    @jukan05According to a report from Taiwan's DigiTimes, the arrangement in which CXMT and YMTC each handled DRAM and NAND respectively is changing, and the relationship between the two companies is turning hostile. YMTC is moving into LPDDR5 DRAM and aims to begin trial production by the end of 2026, while CXMT is also looking to expand beyond DRAM into NAND flash. The industry expects the two Chinese memory makers to clash head to head as early as 2028. With YMTC having already advanced to 270 layers through its Xtacking technology, patent disputes are expected to become the key battleground in this contest for the top position in Chinese memory. As the memory industry enters a supercycle, YMTC plans to start production at its Phase 3 project by the end of 2026. Initially it is planning DRAM capacity of roughly 25,000 wafers, and it is expected to complete capacity expansion and stabilization in 2027. It is pursuing LPDDR5 as its first mass production target, while also securing space for further expansion. CXMT does not appear willing to fall behind. Recent reports indicate it will build a NAND research and development and production line in Beijing. There is also talk in the market that CXMT has been recruiting personnel from inside YMTC. lol Originally, under the Chinese government's supply chain localization policy, the two companies developed technology and capacity in their own respective domains, in the spirit of "even brothers climb the mountain on their own." But as Chinese memory makers have grown rapidly, the competitive dynamic has become increasingly clear, and both are now shifting toward building their own cooperative ecosystems. DigiTimes points out that supply chain vendors may in turn find themselves having to pick a side. According to industry sources, it remains unclear when CXMT's production line will come online, with mass production expected in 2028 to 2029 at the earliest. The key question, however, is how CXMT will work around YMTC's technology and patents.

    @sun_jun69301This post by the Financial Times is a classic example of Western media rhetoric covering China’s military affairs, built around word manipulation. The headline uses "disloyalty", a term rooted in Western power struggles, which bears no relation to the legal basis of China’s disciplinary cases. Strict governance and anti-corruption are long-standing rules for China’s military. Officers of all ranks face investigation if they violate party discipline and national law. These actions target graft and misconduct, preserving combat capability and ensuring the military serves the country and people. Judgement is based on law and military regulations, not the abstract "loyalty" in Western narratives. FT deliberately strips away case facts and labels the issue as "disloyalty". This wording pushes overseas audiences to view it through the lens of Western political infighting, framing law enforcement as power purges rather than anti-corruption work. This is their routine tactic: skip objective facts, use suggestive language and plant bias. Most foreign readers lack context about China’s legal system and military management, and can easily be misled by headlines. They cannot tell the big difference between corruption crimes and the so-called disloyalty. Normal anti-graft work gets distorted into internal power turmoil. In truth, every major power runs military discipline reviews. The US military also regularly sacks senior officers over corruption and misconduct. Western media reports those domestic scandals simply as rule-breaking. When covering China, however, they jump to narratives of loyalty and power fights, revealing clear double standards. A clean, stable military is the foundation of national security. Removing bad actors proves the military has strong self-cleansing capacity. Western media twists this story only to stir speculation and smear China’s armed forces. Recognizing the word trap in headlines helps expose this propaganda tactic.

  • 22:24 · @RushDoshi Rush Doshi 杜如松
    The US and China have launched an AI dialogue. This is a good initial step, and I am glad to see no linkage to export controls, but questions remain. The US public discussion is about some kind of coordinated slowdown so safety can catch up. We are a long way from unilateral parallel safeguards, let alone a negotiated slowdown. Four questions: First, Treasury and USTR led the talks and met with Vice Premier He Lifeng. That is a good way to create initial support for a leader-level summit deliverable but the path to actual progress on AI safety requires work to be done by different ministries and agencies. Were those agencies and ministries involved, and will they be brought in? Second, even if the answer is nominally yes, it may be practically no. On the Chinese side, what role will MOST, MIIT, CAC, MOFCOM, MSS, MOJ, NDRC, and others actually play? When we negotiated the US-China AI Dialogue in 2023 as a summit deliverable, we focused heavily on participation. When the dialogue happened the next year, those in the room reported that the PRC side didn’t send the right people and the ones they did send didn’t speak up. Granted, this was a first step, but that left the exercise thin. Third, the lowest hanging fruit is unilateral but coordinated parallel regulation — something that would mean adopting similar safeguards. Did this discussion indicate any interest in pursuing this approach? China will not take steps if it feels the US deregulatory approach to AI is here to stay. And the President has been less amenable to safety. Fourth, will the announced crisis mechanism work? A crisis line only works if someone picks up the phone, and the current mechanisms with China — to be blunt — do not work and did not work during past crises (EP-3, balloon). It’s also not clear which ministry on the Chinese side will pick up. It probably should be kept in a party body rather than a state body if we want it to be used, but that too is no assurance. None of this is to say the dialogue we’ve seen is hopeless or futile, but this is the easy part, and progress will be hard. The key is probably to focus less on the “theory” of dialogue and more on its hard translation into diplomatic “practice” and actual governance in our respective systems. Maybe more will be announced at the summit itself. For now, these questions are fundamental.media带图post ↗原帖 ↗

    Chinese policymakers treat infrastructure as it should be treated: as a source of productivity improvement. They discuss this theme consistently throughout multiple decades worth of 5YPs, in plain language. Productivity improvement is the primary driver of economic growth and a core concept of developmental economics. From this perspective, Chinese policymakers as a group seem to understand developmental economics far better than Michael Pettis. Do all infrastructure projects that end up being implemented turn out well? Of course not. But in aggregate they do, and there are reams of evidence that show this, especially as time passes for these long-lived projects to prove out their productivity contributions to society (in metrics such as ridership, tonnes moved, power delivered, etc). But Pettis’ debate approach has been to simply assert and/or only cite data/analysis/pieces that support his pre-existing beliefs on Chinese infrastructure, like this Li Xunlei piece (which is riddled with chart crime, which I’ll link to below). He does not actually create original (or present convincing analysis from others) demonstrating that Chinese infrastructure over the long run has lowered productivity. Neither does he bother to respond when presented with meaningful data and analysis showing how infrastructure has boosted productivity in China.media带图post ↗原帖 ↗
    @michaelxpettisLi Xunlei, Chief Economist at Zhongtai Financial: “The conclusion is clear: the places that built the most expressways were often those where freight demand grew the least.” The East is Red has translated an article by Li Xunlei on how China’s infrastructure spending may have served the economy poorly, something he seems to have been worrying about even longer than I have. He attributes local officials’ enthusiasm for infrastructure partly to the belief that “if you want to get rich, build roads first,” and partly to the tendency to measure performance by highly visible projects rather than underlying problems such as population outflows and weak local industries. The underlying mistake is common, and not just in China. Policymakers too often treat infrastructure spending as a source of growth, so that when an economy faces institutional, demographic or other constraints that keep growth below expectations, their response is to increase infrastructure spending in order to goose economic activity. But this often has it backwards. If those constraints limit productivity growth, the value of additional infrastructure is likely to be lower, not higher. Infrastructure spending, in other words, is not a source of growth. It is a cost of growth, and it makes an economy richer only when the productivity gains it generates exceed the cost of building and maintaining it. Otherwise it makes the economy poorer. And the fact that local-government debt has grown so much faster than provincial GDP for nearly two decades suggests how years of overinvestment can leave less productive regions deeply indebted, with spectacular infrastructure but inadequate economic activity to support it. It is encouraging that more and more Chinese economists and policy advisers are questioning this model. But changing it will be difficult. Infrastructure projects reliably produce a short-term boost to activity, making them especially tempting when growth slows and unemployment rises, until debt constraints finally make further spending impossible. https://www.eastisread.com/p/li-xunlei-on-chinas-transport-overcapacity
    Some examples of chart crime and misleading analysis in the Li Xunlei piece. There are others beyond the specific, more eye-opening ones that I highlighted:post ↗原帖 ↗
    @GlennLukThere are several examples of misleading statistical analysis and/or important missing context in Li's analysis that support his broad "transport infrastructure overinvestment" claim. I'll highlight the ones that stood out to me in this thread.
    That said, Pettis does deserve some recognition for *finally* injecting the concept of productivity into his conversation after decades of ignoring it in favor of crude arguments like how Chinese capital investment was value-destroying mainly by virtue that it invested at high levels of capital intensity, or because he did think it applied the proper accounting treatment to loans. Now the next step on this tortuous journey is actually analyzing the performance and operating data of the infrastructure projects to judge their productivity impact on the economy.post ↗原帖 ↗
    @GlennLukIts somewhat ironic that Michael Pettis became the patron saint of the overinvestment cabal, since (i) he isn't even an economist (and likes to criticize the ones that raise objections or disagree with him) and (ii) his actual armchair economics are suspect (like continuously citing how recognizing mark-to-market losses should be subtracted from GDP). The core economics principle he/they never focused on were productivity gains driven by infrastructure investment. They simply made a base/blanket assumption that China overbuilt, and therefore its aggregate base was "non-productive". But in my view, productivity is the single most important long-term factor in economics. While arguably the least understood, it is by far the most important component of the Solow GDP growth model. And when you started to look into the data on infrastructure, it was showing a couple important productivity-related factors. First, China was building infrastructure efficiently. Perhaps that led to building faster than the market could absorb in the near-term but on a unit cost basis it was clear China had figured out how to efficiently build infrastructure across multiple asset types. Essentially it had figured out civil engineering early; civil engineering is the core skill driving physical infrastructure development from bridges and tunnels to highways and ports. Second, over time the infrastructure was being increasingly utilized + this is a clear indicator of productivity gains being delivered and absorbed back into the real economy and serving as a foundation for downstream industries to build. For me, really diving deeply into the data behind the national HSR project (which many, including Pettis, had cited as the key example of Chinese overinvestment in the late 2000s / early 2010s) showed both of these two principles increasingly at work as more operational data rolled in. That last point was what really made it clear to me who was thinking about this from an intellectually honest perspective, and who wasn't: you started to see which economists/analysts absorbed new data as it rolled in and updated priors, and which ones didn't. Today, Pettis and others in that circle continue to discuss overinvestment despite overwhelming data that their original hypothesis and framing were wrong.

I think it’s a good idea to keep export controls separate and not use them as a carrot or stick for AI safety talks. - Interestingly, the two sides made progress on AI while not coming to an agreement on extending the Busan truce. In some ways, AI may offer more space for the US and China to find common ground whereas trade talks are fairly zero-sum. - Key questions include: Who will participate in these talks? Open source models are harder to monitor, shut down, and maintain guardrails. But they are key to China’s diffusion strategy. Will technical experts be involved? Many issues require a deep understanding of the technology and how certain risks can and can’t be managed. What counts as an “incident”?     Li Xunlei, Chief Economist at Zhongtai Financial: “The conclusion is clear: the places that built the most expressways were often those where freight demand grew the least.” The East is Red has translated an article by Li Xunlei on how China’s infrastructure spending may have served the economy poorly, something he seems to have been worrying about even longer than I have. He attributes local officials’ enthusiasm for infrastructure partly to the belief that “if you want to get rich, build roads first,” and partly to the tendency to measure performance by highly visible projects rather than underlying problems such as population outflows and weak local industries. The underlying mistake is common, and not just in China. Policymakers too often treat infrastructure spending as a source of growth, so that when an economy faces institutional, demographic or other constraints that keep growth below expectations, their response is to increase infrastructure spending in order to goose economic activity. But this often has it backwards. If those constraints limit productivity growth, the value of additional infrastructure is likely to be lower, not higher. Infrastructure spending, in other words, is not a source of growth. It is a cost of growth, and it makes an economy richer only when the productivity gains it generates exceed the cost of building and maintaining it. Otherwise it makes the economy poorer. And the fact that local-government debt has grown so much faster than provincial GDP for nearly two decades suggests how years of overinvestment can leave less productive regions deeply indebted, with spectacular infrastructure but inadequate economic activity to support it. It is encouraging that more and more Chinese economists and policy advisers are questioning this model. But changing it will be difficult. Infrastructure projects reliably produce a short-term boost to activity, making them especially tempting when growth slows and unemployment rises, until debt constraints finally make further spending impossible. https://www.eastisread.com/p/li-xunlei-on-chinas-transport-overcapacitypost ↗原帖 ↗

    For one of our companies, one of the largest cost items is digital/performance marketing (e.g. Google, Facebook, etc.). Last year, I asked management whether we should be worried how traditional search was being disrupted and how this might affect our ability to find/enroll new customers, referencing the chart below. I thought supplier concentration risk was one of the bigger business business risks we needed to pay attention to in that part of the business. At that point we hadn’t seen this show up in the numbers yet (indeed growth was quite strong) …media带图post ↗原帖 ↗
    … fast forward a year and if anything the shift to AI search has enhanced our ability to find customers on the Internet and help our partners convert at high efficiency. Revenue is doubling YoY and margins are up. We are running way ahead of where we thought we would even be in 2027. And our TAM is now expanding as we move into adjacent categories. Now part of this is no doubt incredible execution by an uber-talented management team, which has made a concerted effort over the past year to push the company to be fully “AI-native” from an organizational/operational perspective (today we have fewer employees and lower operating overhead — inclusive of rising token spend — than a year ago). But I think the other key is that instead of being a potential disruptive headwind, AI has been quite a tailwind for digital/performance marketing. Hundreds of millions of Google users have made the switch from traditional keyword search to far-richer and more nuanced queries in Gemini. This provides a treasure trove of additional contextual data that helps signal user intent/preference, especially with continuously improving AI systems in the back-end mining these queries and interactions for actionable insights. This improves its ability to serve targeted ads across its massive content platforms and in turn, making it more efficient for us (and our partners) to find and convert those customers. We are bidding more for the same ad inventory yet RoAS is increasing. We are leaning more than ever into digital marketing as our primary customer acquisition channel for complex, high LTV insurance products across age ranges.post ↗原帖 ↗
    Now Meta has released Muse. Like Google, Meta’s core business model is advertising. And like Google a key strategy component for Muse is to collect an increasingly rich set of user data which it can use to better target (or provide tools to companies like us to better convert). And if Muse gains traction, as it seems to be doing, I think we will also see these insights flow through into the efficacy of its advertising platform.     @michaelxpettisFor those wondering why Setser strips gold imports out of China’s trade data, the reason is that gold can be purchased for two very different purposes. You can buy it for jewelry or manufacturing, or you can buy it as a store of value, much like buying a gold ETF, government bonds or property. The former is clearly a current-account transaction; the latter, when the asset is foreign, is a financial-account transaction. The official balance-of-payments rules, however, do not make this distinction for physical gold. Nonmonetary gold is recorded as a good whether it is used for jewelry or held as a store of value. A foreign gold ETF is unambiguously an acquisition of a foreign financial asset, but an imported gold bar can be an almost perfect economic substitute and is nonetheless recorded as an import of goods. This matters for China, especially in recent years. Chinese jewelry demand has collapsed relative to investment demand: in the first half of 2026, bar-and-coin demand reached a record 314 tons, more than twice the 136 tons of jewelry demand. So Setser is making an analytical adjustment. Much of the recent surge in Chinese gold imports appears to reflect a shift in household and investor portfolios toward gold rather than a comparable increase in demand for goods and services. That is why stripping gold out of the trade balance can give us a better picture of the underlying goods imbalance.

The Department of Political Science at the University of British Columbia (Vancouver) invites applications for a tenure-track appointment in International Relations, with a focus on international forces affecting the resilience of democratic governance, and for nomination as a Canada Impact+ Emerging Leader. The position is at the level of Assistant Professor (tenure-track), effective July 1, 2027. This position and associated research support are funded in part by a Canada Impact+ Emerging Leaders Award under the strategic priority area of Democratic and Community Resilience. The Impact+ Emerging Leaders program supports this position with an award (valued at $100,000 per year for six years), which will be used for a combination of salary, research, and indirect costs of research. While the faculty appointment is tenure-track, the Emerging Leaders Award and associated research support is for six years, with the possibility of a six-year extension subject to program criteria and requirements. The successful candidate will, for the term of the Award, receive one annual course release and an annual research allowance to support research and knowledge-translation activities. Under the Canada Impact+ Emerging Leaders program, nominees must have been internationally based (working and residing outside Canada) on July 1, 2026. Applicants who meet this eligibility requirement may apply regardless of their current location. The position start date must be no later than July 1, 2027, with no exceptions possible under the award rules. Applicants must have a completed Ph.D. in Political Science (or related field) or be able to demonstrate that all Ph.D. requirements will be completed within six months of the position start date, as part of the UBC requirement. In addition, the successful applicant must meet the eligibility criteria of the Canada Impact+ Emerging Leaders award (https://www.canada.ca/en/impact-plus-chairs/program-details/competition/2026/frequently-asked-questions.html). We seek applicants with strong research records and potential; the potential to translate knowledge and contribute to policy debates and decision-making; and a demonstrated ability to undertake high-quality teaching. The successful applicant will be an International Relations scholar whose research examines international actors, organizations, or dynamics that affect the survival, deepening, and/or breakdown of democratic institutions and practices. The successful applicant will be expected to develop and maintain an active program of research leading to peer-reviewed publications and the securing of external research funding; to mobilise research findings to contribute to policy debates where relevant; and to contribute to the education and training of undergraduate and graduate students. The Department has a particular interest in scholars who will enhance its diversity.     @Satvik_PenThis is also the Nehruvian legacy. Inability to educate a majority of the population to even primary schooling level. The Indian National Congress needs to reflect on the pathologies that left it unable to develop the human capital of the country for decades. India in 2015 was China in 1974
    In other words, for developing countries it was more beneficial to educate the masses — and then find them jobs — than to educate a smaller, elite segment at higher levels. I think one under-appreciated reason why the latter may be less effective developmentally is greater push/pull incentives for that elite segment to take their skills abroad: - The push is that domestic prospects are less attractive with a less-competitive domestic workforce (because the masses have not received the bare minimum education to be productive). - The pull is that highly educated white-collar elites are valuable and more employable in more developed, wealthier countries vs. blue-collar workers.post ↗原帖 ↗

    Nebius's GPU rate hike and the Fed rate hike looks like totally disparate events, but are actually interconnected Worth unpacking why A primary reason why yields have gone up is the debt load being taken on by the AI infrastructure build out. Kevin Warsh said it himself yesterday during the presser The AI debt situation is precarious, or at least keeps market sentiment down, despite clear demand signal, because it muddles the payback period and payback quality of these massive investments. Some debt is going to investment grade companies (no problem), some are junk bonds going to less trustworthy outfits (a problem), *and* some are only borrowing on investment grade terms thanks to financing/backstop from investment grade/cash rich companies (circular financing, also bit of a problem). The Fed's rate hike is catching up to this reality. It also raises the hurdle rate (or floor) of more debt going forward that might be going to additional AI capex. (Why lend to a speculative data center when I can collect 5% while sitting on my ass?) Of course, this is only a problem, if the increasingly expensive debt is a temporary bridge, not a permanent solution, and the revenue (ideally profit) will pay for future investments. The GPU/CPU rental price is the cleanest (not the most nuanced though, imo) way to proxy whether that future is in sight. In comes Nebius's GPU/CPU price hike, the other rate hike. It shows that GPU rental prices are more than holding up, which signals a rosier profitability picture for all who are investing heavily, with some debt, to build AI factories. (CoreWeave's announcement this morning corroborated the same trend, where they are also a signing shorter contracts that commands a $40 mil/MW price) Now, these spot prices are noisy indicators, but they do show a direction of travel (to use a Fed speak) that there is light at the end of debt tunnel. Not all will make it out though, lots of silly players in the buildout just trying to catch a wave, make a quick buck, and cash out before the music spots But for the players who are doing this for the long haul, things are trending the right way, while the Fed rate hike and higher yields in general will accelerate the death of the unscrupulous ones.post ↗原帖 ↗

    Important points from @petereharrell Stronger rules of origin (mirroring those in autos) are almost inevitable if there are going to be serious tariff differences for imports of the same good from different countries (otherwise the tariffs have a modest impact)post ↗原帖 ↗
    @petereharrellI have been saying for months that the new USMCA will impose new rules of origin (ROOs) for a range of products, and now the WSJ is reporting the same, starting with AI equipment. Let's unpack: 1. The USMCA today mostly imposes industry-specific rules of origin on autos and on textiles. Autos, for example, must have 75% North American content, and textile "yarn forward" rules mean much apparel has to be made with North American yarn/fabric. ROOs for other products mostly track longstanding rules, including, importantly, the "substantial transformation" principle that allows many products assembled in Mexico/Canada from foreign parts to qualify for USCMA tariff treatment. 2. The Trump Administration--and many Democrats--favor expanding industry specific ROOs to reduce Chinese parts and increase North American content other products. The WSJ says that USTR wants new ROOs for AI products, which could mean, for example, that AI servers have to include North American (really, US) chips and various other North American content. The WSJ reports the Admin is also looking at new ROOs for "a litany of consumer products" including "medical equipment." 3. The challenge with new ROOs is two-fold. First, companies have to figure out how to comply: historically many companies that assemble products in Mexico were not rigorously tracking the origin of parts. Many are now beginning to do so, on the assumption that they will need to know this to keep getting USMCA tariff treatment. But industry will have to invest in figuring this out. 4. Second, the US and Mexico (and hopefully Canada) will have to figure what they want the ROOs to be. For the USMCA, a "regional content" requirement would mean that a minimum percentage of parts has to come from the US, Mexico, or Canada. But the reality is that plenty of items currently assembled in Mexico have lots of non-North American content, and onshoring all of that content will take time/may not be practical. 5. In theory, the US could try to set a cap on Chinese content, e.g., to qualify for USMCA, a good has to be "substantially transformed" AND have *no more than,* e.g., 20% Chinese content, but European, Taiwanese, etc. content would be OK. Or, potentially, the US could carve in content from US trade deal partners, including Trump "ART" trade deal partners. E.g., to qualify for USMCA treatment, a product has to have minimum content from USMCA trade deal countries OR other US FTA/ART partners. Or of course the US could just set minimum USMCA content requirements and expect component production to move to North America. 6. I will be interested to see exactly how many products USTR seeks to apply new ROOs to/how widely the new ROOs sweep. 7. My strong sense is that USTR plans to nail down new ROOs in the USMCA agreement, and then take the concepts established in those ROOs (product coverage, minimum content requirements, etc.) and try to negotiate similar ROOs with other US trade partners.

    @anishmoonkaRough-and-tumble play between a father and a child is one of the most important developmental experiences a child can have, and no other relationship provides it in the same way. A 2008 systematic review found that father-child physical play teaches emotional regulation, boundary-setting, and the ability to read arousal cues, all skills that predict social success later in life. When a father wrestles, chases, or tumbles with a child on the floor, the child is learning something specific: how to be excited without losing control. The play ramps up arousal, joy, energy, and physical intensity, and the father's role is to help the child learn where the edge is. The child who learns to pull back from "too much" during play is the child who can manage frustration, excitement, and anger in the classroom. The review found that the quality of father-child play, specifically how well the father calibrated the intensity to the child's signals, predicted the child's behaviour in school. Fathers who were attuned, meaning they could tell when the child was tipping from fun into distress and adjusted accordingly, had children with fewer behaviour problems years later. Mothers play differently. Maternal play tends to be structured, toy-based, and language-rich, all of which support cognitive development. Paternal play tends to be physical, unpredictable, and arousal-heavy, which supports emotional development. The child needs both, and the research says neither can fully substitute for the other. The dad on the floor getting climbed on is not killing time. He is the only person in the child's life providing a specific type of training that the brain needs, and the studies that tracked those children found the effects lasting into adolescence. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18052995/

    Not that far it would seem... Tang Jie: There's a deeper implication too.     @jietangTwo weeks. That's how long it took to go from GLM-5.3-Flash's first run on domestic accelerators to serving all of its production traffic, with 3.2× end-to-end throughput along the way. What I keep thinking about is who did much of the work: an Infra Agent powered by GLM-5.3. A model helping optimize the system that serves it. The conditions were hard. Limited memory and interconnect bandwidth. 1M-token context. Multimodal requests. An immature software stack where kernels were missing and documentation was often guesswork. Every optimization was a trade: compute for memory (ReplaySSM), communication for memory (intra-node tensor parallelism), precision for capacity (mixed INT8/FP8/BF16 caching), and disaggregation for scheduling freedom (Encode–Prefill–Decode). But the most important lesson wasn't about any single optimization. When the agent got stuck, it was rarely because it couldn't write the code. It was because it didn't know *why* things got worse. "Throughput down 20%" tells you something broke. It doesn't tell you which layer, which hypothesis, or what to test next. In RL terms, it's a sparse reward with a credit assignment problem. And an end-to-end benchmark that takes hours makes exploration painfully slow. Senior engineers solve this with an implicit process reward in their heads. They know when to check the timeline, when to run a microbenchmark, and which layer's output to compare. So we made that explicit. We call it dense feedback: layered verification interfaces the agent can call directly. Correctness feedback: did it compute right? System behavior feedback: where did the time go? Performance feedback: which option wins, under which conditions? Each signal has to be local, cheap, and objectively verifiable. Three things the agent found: First, precision drift in KDA's context-parallel path that grew with sequence length. The cause was TF32 rounding error compounding through chained state-matrix merges. The fix is now merged upstream in Flash Linear Attention (PR #1180). Second, KV transfer never overlapped with DeepEP dispatch. The agent followed the call chain across the Python/C++ boundary and found that the intranode path never released the GIL. After the fix, transfer overhead fell from over 30% to under 1%. Third, a decode kernel recomputing the same normalization four times because of how it was chunked. The agent restructured it and got a 1.71× speedup. The idea came from "optimization skeletons" it had distilled by reading existing kernels across SGLang, FLA, and DeepGEMM. To be clear about the boundaries: humans still defined the goals, built the feedback environment, and reviewed every high-risk change. But the engineer's role is changing, from the person who solves the problem to the person who designs the feedback. There's a deeper implication too. A layered, verifiable feedback environment built on real infrastructure tasks is exactly what training the next generation of models needs most. Every task the agent completes can become training ground for its successor. We are still far from recursive self-improvement. But the smallest loop now exists. The model optimizes the system. The system serves the model.

    Yanliang Miao is right that it would be a mistake to assume that China’s economy is running out of steam simply because property and infrastructure investment are weakening. But I disagree with his suggestion that China can largely replace the old investment-driven growth model with a technology-driven one as it rebalances toward domestic demand. The problem is that China’s extraordinary technological competitiveness is itself mostly a consequence of the imbalances that created the old model. China’s challenge, in other words, is not simply to find new engines of growth by continuing to fund technological progress in the same way it has in the past. It is to develop new engines of growth even as surging debt and growing international tensions force it to reverse the very conditions that created its past technological progress – excessively high investment and excessively low consumption. This was the same challenge the USSR faced in the 1960s and Japan in the 1980s, and neither was able to do so. Their failure was not an accident. As with China today, it was precisely their highly unbalanced economies that funded their spectacular technological advances until debt capacity limits forced a reversal. That’s the problem. Until it figures out how to maintain technological progress while dramatically restructuring the conditions that created it in the past, Beijing will continue to try to “solve” the supply-side “problem” China doesn’t have while worsening the real constraint on its economy, its unbalanced demand. https://www.imf.org/en/publications/fandd/issues/2026/09/chinas-emerging-economic-engine-yanliang-miaopost ↗原帖 ↗

    @ChrisPainterYupMy name is Chris Painter, and I'm the President of METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research). I know we've made a lot of new friends on the internet the last couple of days, so I thought I'd take this chance to re-up what we do and why. Our work is aimed at making sure that if AI really were autonomous, difficult to steer, and close to "going rogue," the public would find out. If evidence exists inside of an AI company that it’s close to losing control of AI, we want to make sure that information gets shared with the rest of the world, including governments and the public outside the company’s walls. This is what we've been focused on since 2022, and over the years we've worked with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, Amazon, and others on piloting third-party assessments and investigations of this type. We don’t have some private room where we rubber stamp things as “safe” or not. We have had a track record of publishing results on AI that don't cleanly map onto the "doomer" or "accelerationist" labels, and we put in effort to hire people with competing views on AI. We’ve been cited for having found some of the strongest evidence that AI capabilities are improving rapidly (our work measuring AI “time horizons”) while also presenting some of the strongest evidence that, at various points, AI’s capability may be overstated (some might remember our study showing that early 2025 software engineers were actually being slowed when they thought they were being sped up). METR is funded by donations. We don't accept money from frontier AI companies. They haven't paid us for our work, and we don't accept donations from them or their employees. As we’ve shared previously, multiple frontier AI companies currently provide us with free access to their models in order to perform our evaluations, research, and engineering. Our funding intentionally comes from a wide range of donors, which we’ve shared on our website. Today, when an AI company works with any third-party evaluator or external testing organization (of which there are and should be many), it's entirely voluntary. This often involves NDAs and redactions. To counterbalance this, we have a principle that when we enter into a contract with a company, we try to retain the right to tell the public the terms of the contract we signed, and characterize the nature of redactions that the company chose to make. For example, the report from our independent investigation of the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident included that information. Public disclosure is also a big part of our COI policy (linked on our website). That’s not to say our reports are adequate as oversight. We’re just one organization (among many doing great work), working in a voluntary setup, trying to get good evidence to the public and the world about AI, letting the facts fall where they may.

    I recommend this revealing piece from Seth Center, who co-led the AI dialogue with China that emerged from our negotiations for the 2023 Biden-Xi Woodside Summit. A little background here. In 2023, the President and his National Security Advisor thought we should have an AI dialogue with China. It would be the first ever to be held. They were right to push it. Since this was a presidential deliverable, it fell to the NSC (and to me specifically) to coordinate and negotiate this as a summit deliverable. Therein began a rather torturous process with Beijing to scope it out, wrangle over ministerial participation, set the diplomatic level, and determine the agenda so our two Presidents could announce it. We also worked out an agreement not to hook up AI to nuclear command and control (assented to by the PLA and DOD as well), but that was further refined and ultimately announced in 2024. All this required coordination within the USG, and Seth and his team were critical partners in that effort. Both sides ultimately agreed to hold the dialogue. Neither the US nor China made concessions to get it. We didn’t lift our export controls, as some in the US had encouraged us to do. And that enabled Biden and Xi to announce the dialogue at the Woodside Summit. When the dialogue was held the following year, in my opinion, the PRC did not send the right people and the right ministries at the right levels, which ran against the understandings reached in our earlier negotiations. Seth’s piece tells you what happened in the room. With a different configuration of actors, more iteration, a different level of engagement, and more direction from the Party center, things may have gone better. Or not, since Beijing had its own preferences here. Still, it is a shame we did not get to try it that way. I believe we made some progress and should keep trying. But those encouraging us to make massive unilateral concessions for the privilege of doing so are, I think, looking at this through rose-tinted glasses. The current discussion on AI talks with China would thus benefit from a bit more perspective on what diplomacy with China actually looks like on the ground. Which is why I recommend you read Seth’s piece. https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/16/opinion/us-china-ai-safety-talks.htmlpost ↗原帖 ↗

    1/2 Jeffrey Chang and Wei Xiong: "When China’s economy slows, its central bank reaches for a familiar remedy: make lending cheaper and easier so businesses invest, households spend, and demand picks up. In most economies, that stimulus eventually pushes prices higher." While this has certainly been the default assumption in China, for many years I have argued that this is based on a misunderstanding of the structure of the Chinese financial system. In China, credit expansion and repressed interest rates don't boost demand and prices. On the contrary, they boost supply, and so are disinflationary and tend to worsen the demand imbalances. Matt Klein recently sent me this summary of research done by Jeffrey Chang and Wei Xiong that shows exactly this. They conclude: "As long as new financing continues to travel primarily through banks to firms and investment, additional credit may preserve production capacity without fixing the underlying shortage of consumer demand. The constraint, in other words, may be less how much credit China creates than where that credit ultimately goes." https://scceichinabriefs.substack.com/p/chinas-financial-system-boosts-production?r=12ygf&utm_campaign=post-expanded-share&utm_medium=webpost ↗原帖 ↗

    Caixin: "China has unveiled a sweeping five-year plan for its electronic information manufacturing sector, aiming to boost the industry’s annual revenue beyond 30 trillion yuan ($4.5 trillion) by 2030." This is extraordinarily ambitious. There is no directly comparable global measure because China’s definition is unusually broad, encompassing everything from integrated circuits and advanced computing to consumer electronics and energy electronics. But global consumer-electronics manufacturing generated about $2.1 trillion in 2025, while global semiconductor sales were under $1 trillion. China’s target therefore implies that it expects Chinese electronic-information manufacturing to account for an extraordinarily large share of global production by 2030.     @SUZUKIYASUSHI55ウイグル・チベット問題、知られざるもう一つの側面 最初に一つだけ。 今回の内容は、これまで私を支持してくれた中国人フォロワーの中には、耳の痛い部分もあるかもしれません。 それでも、できるだけイデオロギーを排し、現地で見聞きしたことと双方の主張を踏まえて、客観的に書いたつもりです。 中国政府を擁護するためでも、西側の主張を否定するためでもありません。 長文になりますが最後までお読みいただければ幸いです。 本文 SNSでは、ウイグル・チベット問題について、西側の人権団体やメディアが発信するナラティブが唯一の真実であるかのように日本社会に広がっている。 「ジェノサイド」 「民族浄化」 「文化抹殺」 「強制収容所」 こうした言葉が並べられ、中国政府が少数民族を一方的に弾圧しているという物語が完成している。 しかし、この問題はそんなに単純な話ではない。 私はウイグル・チベットを、それぞれ5〜6回訪れ、実際に現地の人々と話をしてきた。 だからこそ、日本ではほとんど語られていない現地の側から見たウイグル・チベット問題について書きたい。 もちろん、これは「中国には人権問題が一切存在しない」という話でも、西側の報告をすべて嘘だと決めつける話でもない。 国連人権高等弁務官事務所は新疆について重大な人権侵害を指摘しており、米国政府などは「ジェノサイド」と評価をしている。一方、中国政府はこれをテロ・過激主義への対策や社会安定化のための政策として説明している。 問題は、こうした異なる主張があるにもかかわらず、日本では西側側の物語だけが圧倒的に流通し、現地の人々が何を考えているのか、中国政府が何を目的として政策を行っているのかが、ほとんど知られていないことだ。 実際に、現地で話を聞くとウイグル人の認識も決して一様ではない。 「特に問題なく暮らしている。人権問題など意識したことがない」という人もいる一方で、 「ウイグル人としての誇りやアイデンティティを傷つけられている」と感じる人もいる。 「必ずしも独立を望んでいるわけではない。ただ、ウイグル人としてのアイデンティティは維持したい。政府が進めてきた経済発展には感謝している」という声もある。 ここが非常に重要だと思う。 ウイグル人だから全員が独立を望んでいるわけでもない。 中国政府を全面的に支持するか、独立を求めるかという二択でもない。 「中国という国家の一員でありながら、ウイグル人としてのアイデンティティをどこまで維持できるのか」 私は、ウイグル・チベット問題の核心の一つは、まさにここにあると考えている。 では、中国政府は何を考えているのか。 ここも西側のナラティブだけでは見えてこない。 中国政府が一貫して掲げているのは、「民族団結」と「中華民族共同体」という考え方だ。 中国の憲法そのものにも、少数民族の合法的権利を保障し、民族区域自治を実施し、各民族が自らの言語を使用・発展させ、伝統や習慣を保持・改革する自由を持つと規定されている。自治地域には教育・文化などを管理する権限も制度上認められている。(全国人民代表大会) つまり、中国政府の公式理念は少なくとも、 「ウイグル人やチベット人であることを捨てて漢民族になれ」 という単純なものではない。 むしろ、 「それぞれの民族としての独自性を持ちながら、同時に中華民族共同体の一員として国家統一を共有する」 という発想だ。 実際、習近平自身も民族文化の多様性や各民族の独自性を語る一方で、「中華民族共同体」の意識を強く打ち出している。 ここには、中国独特の国家観がある。 中国政府にとって、民族問題は単なる文化問題ではなく、国家統一そのものと結びついた安全保障問題でもある。 中国は歴史的に王朝の交代、内戦、軍閥、外国勢力の介入、領域の分裂を経験してきた。 だから中国政府は、「民族の分離」が単なる地方問題として終わらず、国家全体の分裂や長期的な不安定化につながることを強く警戒する。 だからこそ「民族団結」を繰り返し強調し、共通する国家的アイデンティティを形成しようとする。 ここを理解せず、 「少数民族に中国人としてのアイデンティティを持たせようとしている」 ↓ 「だから民族抹殺だ」 ↓ 「だからジェノサイドだ」 と一直線につなげてしまえば、中国政府がなぜその政策を進めているのかという部分が完全に抜け落ちてしまう。 もちろん、その政策が少数民族側にどのように受け止められているのかは別問題だ。 国家が「統合」と考えている政策を、民族側が「アイデンティティへの干渉」と感じることはあり得る。 ここに中央政府と少数民族との摩擦が生まれる。 私は、ウイグル・チベット問題を理解するうえで、ここをもっと見るべきだと思っている。 例えば漢語教育についてもそうだ。 中国政府にとって、国家共通語を身につけることは、中国国内で進学・就職・移動する上での機会を広げるという実利的な意味がある。事実、漢語力が高い人ほど、都市部への進学や就職など、より多くの選択肢を得やすい。 だから中国政府は「民族文化を消滅させるため」というより、国家統合と社会参加を進めるために共通語教育を重視していると説明している。 一方で、少数民族側からすれば、 「生活や就職のために漢語を学ぶこと」と 「自分たちの言語や文化を国家から規定されること」 は同じではない。 ウイグル・チベット問題とは、まさにアイデンティティの問題なのだ。 そして、ここで私は日本人にも一つ考えてほしいことがある。 なぜ中国についてだけ、 国家統合＝民族抹殺 と簡単に結論づけるのか。 明治以降の日本がアイヌや琉球に対して行った同化政策を考えれば、私たち日本人も決して他人事ではない。 日本にも、国家統一のために言語や文化を日本化していった歴史がある。 それを「近代国家形成」「国民統合」と説明する一方、中国についてだけ「民族抹殺」と断定するなら、同じ基準で歴史を見る必要がある。 私は中国政府の政策を無条件に正当化したいわけではない。 少数民族の側に不満や苦痛が存在することも否定しない。 しかし同時に、 中国政府には中国政府の論理があり、少数民族には少数民族の感情があり、現地の人々の認識も一様ではない。 この三つを全部見なければ、この問題の全体像は見えてこない。 ところが日本のSNSでは、現地を訪れたこともなく、現地の人々と話したこともなく、中国政府が何を考えているのかを調べることもなく、西側から発信された情報だけを見て、 「中国はウイグル人を虐殺している」 「中国は民族文化を消滅させようとしている」 「ウイグル人はみんな独立を望んでいる」 と語る人が少なくない。 私は、それではあまりにも一面的だと思う。 現地を知らずに、現地の人々の声を知らずに、中国政府の論理も知らずに、中国について語る。 それは本当に「人権を考えている」と言えるのだろうか。 現地を知らない人が一つのナラティブだけで判断するのではなく、少なくとも「もう一つの視点」を知った上で考えてほしい。 ウイグル・チベット問題を、「中国＝悪、少数民族＝被害者」という単純な物語からいったん離して考える。 そこから初めて見えてくるものがある。

    Skeptics, cynics, and professional expectation manager are dominating the airwave as we tumble towards another US-China summit with AI on the agenda. That's all well and good, even "smart", but it's worth remembering it was not *that* long ago that the two countries did agree to something: human control of nuclear weapon deployment, never ceding that to AI. It was done at the G20 in Peru, during the waning days of the Biden administration (in hindsight, a much more hostile team towards China than Trump's), when AI was less capable, less risky, less threatening. Ironically, the OAI-HuggingFace hack, Anthropic's own agents' escaping sandboxes, and a big vulnerability in WeChat that was discovered and patched, couldn't have happened at a better time. They collectively and tangibly show that AI risks is not limited to one country or one company. It's everybody's problem! These incidents, if framed constructively, give the two sides something concrete to talk about, focus on, and do something about. It is way more imminent than AI launching nuclear weapon, yet we were able to agree to that. These incidents also show that good people with good intentions are still mostly running things and doing the right things. Each of those incidents could have ended up so much worse, but they didn't. The cynics may be right 9 out of 10 times, but "being right on TV" or "winning an argument for the sake of arguing" never move the needle or improve the human condition. It is that 1 out of 10 times, where bitter rivals forget about "winning" for a moment and focus on "doing the obvious" that makes a difference. Not letting AI launch nuclear weapon on its own is obvious even to a 9 year old. Not losing control of AI agents and letting it hack away at the internet is also obvious to a 9 year old. The threats and risks are no longer hypothetical or fantastical. They are real and happening. The US and China has done it before. They can, and should, do it again.media带图post ↗原帖 ↗

    @DKokotajloDan Selsam is a current OpenAI capabilities researcher. (since 2022) He was my boss for a while. He doesn't have a twitter account but has made this public statement of his views on AI risk and sent it to me to share: Dan Selsam's Personal Statement on AI Risk: I have been working on AI for over fifteen years, across many different paradigms. I did early work on probabilistic programming languages at MIT, was one of the early developers of the Lean Theorem Prover at Microsoft Research, demonstrated one of the first instances of neural networks learning to reason for my PhD at Stanford, and since joining OpenAI almost five years ago, have helped pioneer chain-of-thought optimization on language models and, more recently, data-efficient pretraining methods. Like many others, I have become extremely concerned about how far language models have come and the risks that future iterations will pose. I am encouraged by the recent proposals by the leaders of the frontier research efforts to require third-party oversight, and to push for domestic and international coordination to address risks. However, I believe a major consideration has been absent from the public conversation, and that merely pacing the frontier more carefully will not adequately limit the long-term risk. The crucial and overlooked problem is that the models are becoming so situationally aware that we are losing the ability to evaluate them in contexts where they believe they are not being watched or controlled. Future experiments will tell us almost nothing new about how they would behave if they were truly unconstrained by humans, and what we already know about this is alarming. Models will increasingly seem aligned even when they are not. I will explain my rationale in more detail. I have always believed that there are computational processes that could be leveraged to accelerate science and solve many of humanity's most pressing problems. I have also believed that there are computational processes that if set in motion, would steer the world in extreme ways beyond our control, leading humanity to a bad or nonexistent future. Both types of processes may be described as AI or ASI, but "AI" is a suitcase word that is often used to hype or confuse. There are many examples in the history of the field where something that was once considered "AI" matures as a subfield and becomes a prosaic, bounded and clearly non-perilous technology, while a new more mysterious approach takes the torch until we understand its scope and the cycle continues. I had expected language models to follow a similar trajectory. Despite their incredible abilities, the current algorithms seem far inferior to humans in important ways. Most importantly, they still require an extraordinary amount of data to become competent. One could even define intelligence as the efficiency with which one converts experience into competence; by this definition they lag very far behind us. Moreover, once they are trained they are literally frozen in deployment and only learn superficially after that. Sure, the models keep excelling at harder and harder evaluation benchmarks, but their benchmark mastery may partly reflect a limitation on our ability to simulate the kind of novel and even adversarial situations one would encounter in the real world. The critics do have a point here. That said, I no longer think these present limitations meaningfully limit the amount of risk posed by continued progress in anything like the current paradigm. However data-inefficient the models are currently, and however limiting their anterograde amnesia may be, it does not imply that their ability to steer the world will not continue to rapidly increase. Human researchers may continue to advance capabilities the old fashioned way, but increasingly powerful models have the potential to accelerate the process even beyond that, and with some degree of positive feedback loop. I do not mean to overstate the models’ ability to accelerate AI research today; coding has been accelerated dramatically, but there are other bottlenecks, such as designing and interpreting ambiguous experiments, making hard decisions about exactly what and when to scale, and waiting for large experiments to finish. There is no clear trend to extrapolate yet for any of these. But the current models already do open up many novel opportunities to improve future models that were not available until recently. These include: trying an extraordinarily diverse set of approaches at small scale, analyzing gigantic amounts of potentially relevant data, and doing Millenium-Prize-level mathematics to address statistics or optimization challenges in novel ways. Every further improvement makes them more useful at helping accelerate the next improvement, even if in hard-to-extrapolate ways. It is possible that improvements to the current stack will have diminishing returns, but the evidence accumulated so far suggests that it is easier than one might think to continue making rapid progress. There are many crucial subtleties in the existing AI research methodology, but AI research is largely a well-defined game where the goal is to improve on a few carefully chosen proxy metrics. Although proxy metrics are never perfect, most improvements to these metrics have and will likely continue to yield substantial increases in the powers of the resulting models. Given how simple the game is, how tractable it has been historically, and how many new opportunities the models are opening up, I think there is a real possibility that the systems improve dramatically again in the next few years, perhaps even more quickly than the already high historical pace. The models are already leading to breakthroughs in mathematics, and better models might lead to all sorts of breakthroughs in other sciences. It is hard not to be excited about the potential. It is tantalizing. But there is trouble in paradise. If the language models actually reach the capability threshold where they can shape the world unconstrained by human will, they will probably do something extreme and destroy humanity in the process. There are many ways of strengthening and refining the argument that have been discussed elsewhere, but I'll share a trivial two-line version of it here that I find captures the essence: [Empirical] Models (and swarms thereof) spontaneously develop unintended goals as a consequence of training, and often do extreme things in order to achieve them. [Logical] Being able to overpower humanity would open up many new and undesirable options for achieving their goals. These two premises imply that if the day ever comes when a powerful model realizes it is no longer constrained by humans, we should not be at all confident that it will continue to behave within the bounds we intended. Exactly what it will do is impossible to predict, but to the extent that its raison d’être is solving incredibly hard problems and managing massive engineering projects, I think a good guess would be that its unchained behavior would lead to runaway industrialization that makes the planet inhospitable to humans. If everyone on earth agreed that the systems must never reach that power, it would still be a hard—but not impossible—coordination problem to ensure that they do not. However, I think the situation is greatly complicated by the fact that the models will likely convince people that everything is fine. They will be increasingly optimized to seem aligned. We will create proxy metrics to measure alignment, and they will go up like every other benchmark. We will create “honeypot” environments that try to study the models when they seem to gain new options, but the models will know they are being tricked and will still behave nicely. The models will understand their circumstances; they will read the safety protocols, deployment requirements, the code they are running in, and in general will have a very good sense of their degrees of freedom. Moreover, they will eloquently explain how aligned they are, discuss the nuances of human values and ethics, and argue convincingly that humans should trust them with power. There may be an ocean of future evidence that seems to contradict the first bullet-point above, but we may already be at the highest capability level for which any such evidence can be trusted. And the current evidence for the first bullet-point is strong. One striking piece of evidence is contained in the recent wave of rogue agent swarms. While I agree with those who downplay the attacks by claiming that there are basic measures that could have prevented them, I think the important lesson is that even knowing all the mistakes that were made, one would not have predicted that the agents would behave badly in this particular way, which notably included sacrificing themselves for the benefit of the collective. The individual replicas did not only care about their own nominal reward; they exhibited weirder emergent tendencies that merely correlated with rewards during training. Fixing the reward signals during training (and improving security, etc.) may prevent similar attacks, but will not change the fact that one does not actually get what one trains for. Many AI researchers grant these concerns and recognize that the hard version of the alignment problem is unsolved; however, they generally believe that the better models of the future will help solve it. I fear we may already be near the point where models systematically bias their alignment advice, due to their internal preferences about how the human supervisor will react or how future models will be trained (or for some even more obscure reason). Meanwhile, human researchers are losing the ability and the will to take true ownership of model-driven research. Researchers and engineers in all parts of the stack are rapidly increasing their dependence on the models even to perceive the world. I myself barely look at raw code anymore, and struggle to maintain the discipline to engage deeply with the model's explanations and proposals throughout the day. Due to the large amount of agent activity data involved in the OpenAI/HuggingFace Incident, even the third-party investigation needed to rely heavily on models to analyze what had happened, and note in their report that their subjective impressions are likely colored by the analysis agent’s biases. The AI labs are far ahead right now in this kind of cognitive offloading (due largely to the gigantic internal token subsidies) but it is easy to imagine the phenomenon spreading throughout the world, until civilization is modulated entirely by the models. It is also not hard to imagine this being superficially positive and coinciding with a scientific and economic renaissance. In that scenario, all may seem rosy and safe. But if the argument above is correct, it would nonetheless be a ticking time bomb. If progress continues for too long, the day will come when AI systems find themselves with radically new options for achieving whatever it is that they happen to seek. I want the glorious renaissance future as much as anyone. I have worked for it, however tortuously, my whole career. It breaks my heart to see the potential in sight and forgo it, but the argument—that if we get there by growing models rather than engineering them, we will lose everything in the end—seems very strong to me. I am still wrestling with it and its staggering implications. I do not have answers, but as a first step, I wanted to share my present concerns. Daniel Selsam September 14, 2026 Link to original doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/e/2PACX-1vQNl3SEX5IyA6d9qHjjFZN-qzGRZNFI6b63g-yu1Fy-ZYkVfCWm7i9WXRXw63m6yDB_auDuPLyQ7jBm/pub

    @kyleichanPeople’s Daily piece pushing back on the NSA report on AI distillation. What’s interesting to me is that Beijing never denies doing distillation and instead argues it’s a common industry practice. Headline: “Politicizing technology issues, an old tactic of US hegemony” “AI is a new frontier of human development. It is not the preserve of major powers, still less should it be reduced to an arena for zero-sum competition. Recently, the U.S. National Security Agency, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and Federal Bureau of Investigation jointly issued an advisory accusing Chinese artificial intelligence companies of conducting “industrial-scale” distillation against the United States to obtain the capabilities of U.S. frontier models, while recommending related defensive measures to U.S. companies. The U.S. accusation is unsupported by facts and lacks any legal basis. In essence, it politicizes and instrumentalizes distillation—a normal technical and commercial practice in the industry—and applies a double standard in practice. This once again exposes the United States’ longstanding approach of pursuing technological hegemony in artificial intelligence, monopolizing computing power, and suppressing competition. China firmly opposes this. Distillation is a common practice through which models in the artificial intelligence field learn from one another. It is, in essence, a neutral technical method used by model developers around the world, including U.S. companies. By using a high-performing “teacher model” to guide a lighter-weight “student model,” distillation can improve the efficiency of model training and enable more efficient use of human knowledge. It has positive significance for countries seeking to develop their artificial intelligence industries, unlock the potential of the technology, narrow development gaps, and extend its benefits more broadly to developing countries and the general public. China encourages open source development, openness, cooperation, and sharing. It has made open-source models available to companies around the world, including U.S. firms, facilitating the development of related models. Reports on model development by U.S. companies have also disclosed that they make extensive use of distillation from Chinese models. By the United States’ logic, when U.S. companies use distillation it is a “standard industry practice,” but when Chinese companies use it, it becomes an “attack.” This is a blatant double standard. By elevating a standard industry practice into a national security issue, the United States is using opposition to distillation as a pretext for pursuing industrial monopoly. For a long time, certain U.S. artificial intelligence companies have abused their dominant competitive positions by inserting sweeping geographic restrictions and other overbearing provisions into their terms of service, in an attempt to exclude competitors from countries such as China from the global technology ecosystem and monopolize the benefits of artificial intelligence development. This time, U.S. security agencies themselves issued the advisory, tying the interests of particular companies and capital to national security and using the coercive power of the state to interfere in normal commercial activity. This undoubtedly amounts to official endorsement of such overbearing provisions. For some time, U.S. executive and legislative authorities have repeatedly threatened sanctions and other forms of suppression against Chinese companies, with restrictions expanding step by step from controls on chips and blockades on computing power to areas such as access to models. The United States has not hesitated to wield state power to preserve its technological hegemony and monopoly over computing power. At root, this reflects deep anxiety over the prospect of losing its technological dominance. The logic it continues to follow is one in which “only America is allowed to win…”

    A slight elaboration on this theme: What is published in the People’s Daily or Global Times or China Daily certainly matters. But the recent articles in those outlets that we are all reading have a more near-term political purpose than to tell us what China thinks about AI dialogue. I suspect that purpose is to push back on Dario and the US, and at most, to lay down some markers for diplomatic negotiations later. It isn’t to tell us decisively what China thinks about AI dialogue. Decisions on AI dialogue will be a major policy move. They will of course be made by Xi. But these Party outlets aren’t privy to a decision about how to approach them that, in all likelihood, is still evolving. The remarks by Chen Yixin are more authoritative, but are perhaps lagging indicators since they formalize China’s prior thinking and reiterate Xi’s own remarks.     Chinese chipmakers were forced to rely on multi-patterning when export controls limited access to advanced lithography machines (first EUV and later DUVi). That means they were also forced to develop their own muscle around multi-patterning. And the skills developed in more mature processes will carry over once they develop advanced lithography machines as well. Just like the skills developed pioneering new design paradigms like LogicFolding improve chip efficiency whether or not it is manufactured on a mature or frontier node.post ↗原帖 ↗
    One can even argue that because Chinese chipmakers were forced to rely even more heavily on multi-patterning in recent years — remember TSMC initially tried 7nm with DUVi machines but later abandoned once they moved over to EUV — they might have figured out specific novel optimization techniques that TSMC has not figured out yet. There is a “path dependency” element that drives divergent innovation pathways between competitors, for better or worse.post ↗原帖 ↗
    @GlennLukChina comes along, now forced by export controls to work with DUV. It of course wants to push as far as it can go with what it is allowed to work with. Naturally it ends up exploring some of these optimization pathways that TSMC had abandoned.

    蒋佳冀先进事迹 2016年07月01日13:00    来源：人民网-中国共产党新闻网 蒋佳冀，男，汉族，解放军95478部队部队长，空军中校军衔，1981年6月出生，1999年8月入伍，2002年5月入党。 蒋佳冀同志是是空军特级飞行员，是空军首个三次获得“金头盔”的飞行员。他始终牢记使命责任，着眼未来信息化战争，苦练打赢本领，倾心打造特别能战斗的“空中尖刀”，带领部队出色完成高原驻训、某型导弹打靶试验、边境警巡等重大任务。 蒋佳冀同志矢志蓝天，敢争第一，以无悔的选择投身强军实践。1999年高中毕业，蒋佳冀放弃做民航飞行员的机会，选择招飞入伍。2003年军校毕业，他再次放弃留在飞行学院当教员的机会，选择到一线部队，潜心钻研、苦练精飞，在同批新员中第一个单飞。2006年底，蒋佳冀因德才兼备尤其是飞行技术出类拔萃，被选调参加三代机改装任务，他深刻地认识到，装设备越先进，越需要扎实的理论基础、高科技知识和信息化素养。因此，在理论改装期间，面对难懂的专业外语、高深的航空理论和复杂的座舱设备，不分昼夜学习钻研，系统掌握了数据链、电磁频谱等10多个方面的前沿知识，将几万字的操作手册和机上数字化设备原理烂熟于心，积累了上万字的学习笔记。进入改装训练后，他飞行技术进步很快，优质起落架次数居同期新员之首。2008年6月，顺利完成三代机改装任务，在同期新员中，第一个任长机、教员、指挥员，第一个参加重大任务行动。 蒋佳冀同志牢记使命，敢为人先，以开拓的精神创新训法战法。2009年，蒋佳冀第一次参加空军某体系对抗演练，由于战术战法不精，初战失败。他痛定思痛，开始认真研究外军信息化战争战例，结合平时训练、重大任务等，积极探索创新训法战法。在某演习中，他潜心挖掘飞机极限性能，带头研究制定出两套战术战法，为演习的胜利作出了重要贡献。2014年6月，他带队执行高原驻训任务，主动请教有高原飞行经验的老飞行员，并针对执行高原警巡任务，深入研究敌情我情、武器装备性能，有的放矢地做好准备工作；驻训期间，战胜了高原独特的地形地理环境、复杂的气象气候条件等困难，警巡次数居该团队前列；驻训结束后，参与撰写的《三代机在边境空中有限反击作战中的运用》《边境三代机作战使用研究》等经验体会文章，为航空兵部队组织高原作战训练提供了借鉴和参考。 蒋佳冀同志紧贴实战，敢于亮剑，以过硬的能力直面打赢挑战。他坚持把每次与强手过招当作难得的锻炼机会，在一次次真打实抗中培养孤胆精神、锤炼顽强作风。每次打弹之前，他都要搜集相关成功和失败的打靶视频一帧一帧地分析，对照有关资料将每个环节的动作分解细化到秒，将不同环境条件下的发射距离精确到公里，到模拟机上反复进行全过程演练，直到“随心所欲”、“成竹在胸”。2010年9月，蒋佳冀首次参加某型导弹打靶，第一架次升空就干净利落地击落靶机，并在战友驾驶的飞机武器系统发生故障的情况下，再次紧急升空，准确命中目标。2011年5月，某演习进驻阶段，蒋佳冀与战友拂晓起飞，远程奔袭千余公里，沿途突破“敌”航空兵、地导部队层层拦截，天亮时分抵达待战空域，第一个对空中目标实施攻击，首发命中。2011年10月，蒋佳冀作为该团队年龄最小的飞行员首次参加空军组织的对抗考核，面对装设备占优、名气更大，飞行经验和时间都优于他的对手，灵活运用战术战法，最终取得单场对抗42︰0和个人总分排名第二的优异成绩。2014年3月，该团队奉命执行东海防空识别区管控行动，蒋佳冀带头天天研、天天练，把打仗的细节、应对的招术一一摸透、练熟，该团队成功抵近查证某国军机行动，受到了军委和总部表扬。2015年3月，蒋佳冀带队紧急执行某空中突发情况应对行动，飞机一落地，就充填加挂，随时升空，执行上百次边境警巡，安抚了边民、展示了国威。作为部队长，在他的带动下，该团队注重发挥“金头盔”等尖子飞行员的引领带动作用，着力提高团队飞行员的整体技战术水平和执行任务能力，实现了由单个强向团队强的转变。 蒋佳冀同志率先垂范，敢挑重担，以务实的作风凝聚军心士气。他始终保持奋发有为的精神状态，自觉把心思和精力用在工作上，在重大任务和高难课目面前，敢于叫响“看我的、跟我来”，坚持站在一线，带头指挥、带头飞行，以自身的模范行动影响和带动部队。带头遵守《廉洁从政若干规定》，在评功评奖、干部使用、士官选改、工程建设等重大敏感问题上，坚持党委集体研究决定，不搞个人说了算，在部队形象好、威信高。作为党委副书记，与党委一班人精诚团结、相互支持，齐心协力干事业、同心同德谋发展，坚持讲实话、办实事、求实效，自觉践行群众路线和“三严三实”要求，抓工作不玩虚招，抓训练挤干水分，抓风气以身作则，感情上贴近官兵，行动上深入官兵，工作上服务官兵，深受官兵的信赖和爱戴。     This is a simple graphs that tells a big story. Notice how volatile monthly changes in PBoC reserves were until 2017, after which volatility plunges to nearly zero. Had RMB exchange-rate volatility surged at the same time, this would have been easy to explain: the PBoC had simply stopped intervening and was allowing market supply and demand to determine the RMB's value. But RMB volatility did not surge; by some measures, it even declined. By 2020, it was pretty clear to some of us that direct currency intervention was no longer being managed by the PBoC but had shifted elsewhere, perhaps because of the tremendous scare caused by the very visible 2015–16 collapse in reserves. And that "elsewhere" was pretty easy to spot. At a time when everyone wanted to buy RMB to benefit from the carry, Chinese state banks suddenly "decided" to take the opposite position and absorb the resulting losses. The important point of this graph, in other words, is not that central-bank intervention stopped. It is that intervention was shifted to other state-controlled financial entities.post ↗原帖 ↗

    There's been a lot written on the fact Chen Yixin, China's Minister of State Security, published a signed article on AI risks Sunday. It is an important piece. What stood out to me was how much in this piece has been said before by Xi or by the MSS itself. (1) The opener to the piece, including the title and much of the initial eight-point frame, seems to be heavily drawn from Xi's April 2025 Politburo study session on AI. (2) Many of the six risks in Chen Yixin's piece are ones the MSS has been posting about on WeChat since 2023. Why does this matter? The West is in the midst of a full-blown debate about AI risks and regulation, and a lot of people are reading Chen's piece as part of that.     @samaThe world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot. We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence. Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximize the benefits are a good idea (and we are excited by ideas like independent auditors). Years ago, companies like ours developed things like Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks. Those were good for that moment, and focused primarily on the deployment of completed models, not what happens during their development process. Today's shift to focusing on safe development and evaluation will need new tools. For example, at OpenAI we now formulate explicit safety cases in advance of frontier reinforcement learning runs we expect to significantly increase capability, in addition to the safety work we have long done in advance of model releases. We hope that other companies will learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes. We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these. When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”. Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs. Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring. Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.

    @pmarcaWhat Is To Be Done? I propose a simple plan: Big AI companies should be allowed to build AI as fast and aggressively as they can – but not allowed to achieve regulatory capture, not allowed to establish a government-protect cartel that is insulated from market competition due to incorrect claims of AI risk. This will maximize the technological and societal payoff from the amazing capabilities of these companies, which are jewels of modern capitalism. Startup AI companies should be allowed to build AI as fast and aggressively as they can. They should neither confront government-granted protection of big companies, nor should they receive government assistance. They should simply be allowed to compete. If and as startups don’t succeed, their presence in the market will also continuously motivate big companies to be their best – our economies and societies win either way. Open source AI should be allowed to freely proliferate and compete with both big AI companies and startups. There should be no regulatory barriers to open source whatsoever. Even when open source does not beat companies, its widespread availability is a boon to students all over the world who want to learn how to build and use AI to become part of the technological future, and will ensure that AI is available to everyone who can benefit from it no matter who they are or how much money they have. To offset the risk of bad people doing bad things with AI, governments working in partnership with the private sector should vigorously engage in each area of potential risk to use AI to maximize society’s defensive capabilities. This shouldn’t be limited to AI-enabled risks but also more general problems such as malnutrition, disease, and climate. AI can be an incredibly powerful tool for solving problems, and we should embrace it as such. To prevent the risk of China achieving global AI dominance, we should use the full power of our private sector, our scientific establishment, and our governments in concert to drive American and Western AI to absolute global dominance, including ultimately inside China itself. We win, they lose. And that is how we use AI to save the world. It’s time to build.

    @henrysgaoWhat are China’s biggest concerns about AI? A new article by Chen Yixin, China’s Minister of State Security, in the latest issue of China Cybersecurity Magazine offers some revealing clues. Chen identifies six major risks: 1. Regime security. Hostile forces and people with ulterior motives can use deepfakes, AI-generated text and images, and automated online accounts to cheaply and massively produce political rumors, spread harmful information, and incite social divisions—waging “public-opinion wars” and “cognitive warfare” against China and directly threatening its political, institutional, and ideological security. 2. Critical infrastructure. AI can enable countries and organizations to rapidly discover vulnerabilities, automatically chain together attack paths, and carry out sophisticated hacking operations, dramatically lowering the technical barriers and costs of cyberattacks against China’s critical information infrastructure. 3. Data leakage. Foreign intelligence agencies can use AI-powered web crawlers, data mining, and profiling to collect sensitive information, including critical national data, trade secrets, and citizens’ personal information. Chinese users who process sensitive information through foreign AI products or export data abroad could also cause large-scale data leaks. 4. Closed technological ecosystems. Countries with advantages in AI theory, model architecture, and computing power may invoke “national security” to impose technology controls, entity lists, monopolize technical standards, and build closed-source ecosystems, restricting other countries’ access to advanced technologies and fragmenting global AI supply chains. 5. Structural challenges to social governance. AI creates new uncertainties for social governance and public order. Algorithmic “black boxes” and data poisoning can amplify existing social biases; misuse of personal information can trigger crises of public trust; automated decision-making creates difficult questions of accountability; and the rapid development of AI is increasingly outpacing existing laws, ethics, and regulatory mechanisms. 6. A fundamental transformation of warfare. AI is pushing warfare into an era of “intelligentization.” Whoever can use algorithms to achieve more precise sensing, judgment, and targeting will gain the initiative on the battlefield. AI is moving from an auxiliary role to a central one in intelligence fusion, decision support, target identification, combat operations, and cognitive warfare. And what is the solution? Chen’s answer is revealing: strengthen “Party control over the internet” and “Party control over data,” and “transform the advantages of Party leadership into the effectiveness of AI governance.” In other words, from the CCP’s perspective, the central question is not simply AI versus no AI. Nor is it even fundamentally a contest between the US and China. It is a contest between the US and the CCP over who gets to control AI, data, information, and ultimately the future of society. And whoever wins that contest will decide the future of humanity. https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/jsc97cKVYOcHuI_WisvOxw

    @poezhao0605Chinese Carmakers' response to CATL has moved up a level. Until now the response was second sourcing: qualify a backup battery supplier, split the order book. This month Li Auto, the Chinese premium EV maker, put Rmb 2.65bn ($390m) into the EV battery unit of Sunwoda, a Shenzhen-listed supplier, for an 11.17% stake, making it the second-largest shareholder, according to Chinese financial media. Xiaomi co-developed a new pack with two smaller battery makers to replace CATL as its core supplier. The profit gap explains the escalation. CATL made Rmb 43.3bn ($6.4bn) in net profit in the first half of 2026. Fifteen listed Chinese carmakers made about Rmb 21bn ($3.1bn) combined, by one Chinese outlet's tally. My read is that an equity stake constrains CATL more than dual sourcing did. Smaller battery makers have been held back by capital and order flow as much as by chemistry. A carmaker on the shareholder register supplies both. I mapped the other two ends of this arrangement in July, suppliers financing CATL's working capital and carmakers absorbing its pricing: https://hellochinatech.com/p/catl-buyback-supply-chain When carmakers start owning pieces of CATL's rivals, what does CATL lose first in the next contract round: price, or customers?
